title: Checkpoint: Energy and Electricity
objective: After this level you can explain how electricity is made, stored and used to do work.
summary: Generators make electricity, batteries store it as chemicals, and bulbs and motors use it. Power is how fast energy flows: a watt is a joule per second, and a kilowatt-hour is 3.6 million joules.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: what does your electricity bill actually charge for?
cards.body: Not electrons: Level 3 showed they were in your wires all along. You pay for energy, measured in kilowatt-hours. To see what that means, put the whole chapter together.

items.label: Made
points: Generators spin a magnet inside coils (Level 8)

items.label: Used
points: Bulbs turn it into light and heat (Level 5)

cards.headline: Watts: how fast energy flows
cards.body: A watt is one joule of energy every second. Remember Level 2's apple? Lifting one a meter every second takes about a watt. Watts also join Level 3's two ideas: volts times amps equals watts, because joules per coulomb times coulombs per second gives joules per second. A 60-watt bulb uses 60 joules every second it's on.

cards.context: That's 1,000 watts running for an hour (3,600 seconds), and it's the unit utilities measure and charge for. In apples, that's 3.6 million small apples, each lifted a meter. Swap an old bulb for an LED, which uses at least 75% less energy, and the same light takes a quarter or less of the kilowatt-hours.

mascot.line: Your bill is secretly a very long list of lifted apples. I find that oddly comforting.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: Generators make electricity; batteries store energy as chemicals
Bulbs and motors turn electricity into light, heat and motion
A watt is a joule per second: volts times amps

options.label: One coulomb of charge per second
One joule of energy per second
One joule per coulomb of charge
One kilowatt-hour of energy
options.rationale: That's a unit of energy, not power.

questions.explanation: A watt is a rate: one joule of energy every second.

questions.prompt: A device runs on 10 volts and draws 2 amperes. What is its power?

options.label: 5 watts
options.rationale: That divides volts by amps; multiply instead.

options.label: 12 watts
20 watts
200 watts

questions.explanation: Volts times amps equals watts: 10 x 2 = 20 watts, or 20 joules every second.

questions.prompt: Chapter recap: what does a battery do that a power-station generator doesn't?

options.label: It spins a magnet inside coils
It creates brand-new energy
It holds energy as chemicals for later
It turns sunlight straight into current

questions.explanation: A battery stores chemical energy and turns it into electrical energy when the circuit is closed; a generator turns motion into electricity as it spins.

questions.prompt: From Level 3: what does voltage measure?

options.label: How fast electrons drift along the wire
options.rationale: That's drift speed, a meter or two an hour.

options.label: How many electrons pass each second
How hot the wire gets
options.rationale: Heat is a result, not what voltage measures.

options.label: The energy given to each coulomb of charge

questions.explanation: One volt is one joule of energy for every coulomb of charge.

questions.prompt: From Level 9: why is power sent over long lines at high voltage?

options.label: It makes long-distance transmission more efficient
Homes need very high voltage to run
High voltage turns AC into DC
options.rationale: Transformers change voltage, not the type of current.

options.label: It makes the electrons drift faster
options.rationale: The gain is efficiency, not electron speed.

questions.explanation: Higher voltage makes long-distance transmission more efficient and cheaper; transformers lower it again for homes.
